lead: Two phases touch at an interface. The gas and liquid are not in equilibrium in their bulk, but they are in equilibrium at the interface itself. Solute crosses a gas film and a liquid film in series. The two-resistance theory uses this picture to find the interface composition, the flux, and which film controls. It is the working method behind absorber and stripper calculations, and it explains why ammonia leaves air into water easily while oxygen does not.
prereq: You need individual and overall mass transfer coefficients, and the idea of an equilibrium line y* = m x from solubility data.

blocks.text: Let y be the solute mole fraction in the bulk gas and x the solute mole fraction in the bulk liquid. At the interface these become y<sub>i</sub> and x<sub>i</sub>. The two-resistance model makes three assumptions. First, the gas and liquid at the interface are in equilibrium, so y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>. Here m is the slope of the equilibrium line y = m x on a mole-fraction plot. Second, no solute accumulates at the interface. Third, the same flux N<sub>A</sub> passes through both films.

Each film carries flux with its own coefficient: N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>y</sub>(y − y<sub>i</sub>) = k<sub>x</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> − x). k<sub>y</sub> is the gas-film coefficient and k<sub>x</sub> the liquid-film coefficient, both in kmol/(m²·s) per unit mole-fraction difference. The equality is the key equation. It says the gas-side driving force (y − y<sub>i</sub>) and the liquid-side driving force (x<sub>i</sub> − x) adjust until the two fluxes match.

items: Write the interface equilibrium relation y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>.
Substitute into the equal-flux equation: k<sub>y</sub>(y − m x<sub>i</sub>) = k<sub>x</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> − x).
Put either side back into the flux equation to get N<sub>A</sub>.

blocks.text: On the y-x plot the interface is where the equilibrium line meets a straight line from the bulk point (x, y). That line has slope −k<sub>x</sub>/k<sub>y</sub>, because (y − y<sub>i</sub>)/(x − x<sub>i</sub>) = −k<sub>x</sub>/k<sub>y</sub>.

blocks.where: N<sub>A</sub> is the solute flux in kmol/(m²·s); k<sub>y</sub> is the gas-film coefficient in kmol/(m²·s); k<sub>x</sub> is the liquid-film coefficient in kmol/(m²·s); y and x are bulk mole fractions; y<sub>i</sub> and x<sub>i</sub> are interface mole fractions.

blocks.text: Designers prefer one driving force, not two. Define y* = m x: the gas mole fraction that would be in equilibrium with the bulk liquid. Define x* = y/m: the liquid mole fraction that would be in equilibrium with the bulk gas. Then the overall gas driving force is y − y*, and the overall liquid driving force is x* − x.

Write N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*) and N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>x</sub>(x* − x). K<sub>y</sub> and K<sub>x</sub> are overall coefficients. They are built from the film coefficients by adding resistances in series.

blocks.where: K<sub>y</sub> is the overall gas-phase coefficient in kmol/(m²·s); k<sub>y</sub> and k<sub>x</sub> are the individual film coefficients; m is the slope of the equilibrium line y = m x.
K<sub>x</sub> is the overall liquid-phase coefficient in kmol/(m²·s); the other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: The factor m appears because k<sub>x</sub> uses Δx while K<sub>y</sub> uses Δy. This is why k<sub>y</sub> and k<sub>x</sub> cannot simply be added. The gas-film share of the total resistance is (1/k<sub>y</sub>)/(1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>). The liquid-film share is (m/k<sub>x</sub>)/(1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>).

Read the shares before designing. If the gas share is near 1, the gas film controls: changing gas turbulence helps, changing liquid mixing hardly helps. If the liquid share is near 1, the liquid film controls. Ammonia in water is gas-film controlled: ammonia is very soluble, m is small, and m/k<sub>x</sub> is small. Oxygen in water is liquid-film controlled: oxygen is sparingly soluble, m is large, and m/k<sub>x</sub> dominates. The same reasoning tells you where to spend pressure drop and packing.

sections.h3: Reading the plot and checking the answer

blocks.text: The figure uses y = 2x, bulk gas y = 0.10, bulk liquid x = 0.02, k<sub>y</sub> = 0.05 and k<sub>x</sub> = 0.08 kmol/(m²·s). The bulk point is above the equilibrium line, so solute goes from gas to liquid. The interface point (0.03667, 0.07333) sits on the equilibrium line. Notice that x<sub>i</sub> > x and y<sub>i</sub> < y: the interface is richer in solute than the bulk liquid and poorer than the bulk gas. That is how both films keep positive driving forces.

The tie line from (0.02, 0.10) to (0.03667, 0.07333) has slope −0.08/0.05 = −1.6. Check: (0.07333 − 0.10)/(0.03667 − 0.02) = −1.6. Any other interface point on y = 2x would give unequal fluxes. The equality of fluxes picks exactly one point.
Use the same check in exams: compute N<sub>A</sub> from the gas side and from the liquid side. They must match. If they do not, you have mixed bulk and interface values, or forgotten m.

figure.caption: The worked example on the y–x diagram. A line of slope −k<sub>x</sub>/k<sub>y</sub> = −1.6 from the bulk point (0.02, 0.10) meets the equilibrium line y = 2x at the interface (0.0367, 0.0733). The overall driving forces use y* = 0.04 and x* = 0.05. All three routes give 1.333×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s).

examples.question: In an absorption column, bulk gas y = 0.10 and bulk liquid x = 0.02 (mole fractions). The equilibrium line is y* = 2x. The individual coefficients are k<sub>y</sub> = 0.05 kmol/(m²·s) and k<sub>x</sub> = 0.08 kmol/(m²·s). Find the interface compositions and the flux.
steps: At the interface, equilibrium holds: y<sub>i</sub> = 2 x<sub>i</sub>.
Gas-side flux: N<sub>A</sub> = 0.05(0.10 − 0.07333) = 1.333×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s). Liquid side gives the same: 0.08(0.03667 − 0.02) = 1.333×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s).

Check with the overall coefficient: 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/0.05 + 2/0.08 = 45, so K<sub>y</sub> = 0.0222 kmol/(m²·s); y* = 2 × 0.02 = 0.04, and K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*) = 0.0222 × 0.06 = 1.333×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s), the same flux without any interface values.
examples.check:
k<sub>y</sub> = 0.05
k<sub>x</sub> = 0.08
y = 0.10
x = 0.02
m = 2.0
x<sub>i</sub> = (k<sub>y</sub>*y + k<sub>x</sub>*x)/(k<sub>y</sub>*m + k<sub>x</sub>)
y<sub>i</sub> = m*x<sub>i</sub>
N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>y</sub>*(y - y<sub>i</sub>)
print(round(x<sub>i</sub>, 5))
print(round(y<sub>i</sub>, 5))
print(round(N<sub>A</sub>, 6))

traps: Assuming the bulk gas and bulk liquid are in equilibrium. Equilibrium holds only at the interface; y* = m x is a hypothetical gas in equilibrium with the bulk liquid, not the actual bulk gas.
Mixing interface and bulk values: using y* = m x<sub>i</sub> instead of y* = m x, or y<sub>i</sub> = m x instead of y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>.

Adding k<sub>y</sub> and k<sub>x</sub> directly. They use different driving forces, so the m factor must appear: 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>, not 1/k<sub>y</sub> + 1/k<sub>x</sub>.
Placing the interface point off the equilibrium line. It lies on the equilibrium line, exactly where the line of slope −k<sub>x</sub>/k<sub>y</sub> drawn from the bulk point meets it.
Forgetting units: k<sub>y</sub> and k<sub>x</sub> are in kmol/(m²·s) per unit mole-fraction difference, and mole fractions have no unit. Check that each N<sub>A</sub> comes out in kmol/(m²·s).

quiz.q: State the three assumptions of the two-resistance theory.
quiz.a: The two phases are in equilibrium at the interface, there is no accumulation at the interface, and the same flux passes through both films.

quiz.q: Why is equilibrium assumed only at the interface and not in the bulk phases?
quiz.a: The bulk phases are separated by the films; solute is still crossing them. Equilibrium at the interface fixes the interface compositions, while the bulk compositions are set by the column flow and are not in equilibrium.

quiz.q: At 25 °C, y = 0.08, x = 0.01, m = 1.5, k<sub>y</sub> = 0.04 kmol/(m²·s), k<sub>x</sub> = 0.10 kmol/(m²·s). Find x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub> and N<sub>A</sub>.
Ammonia in water is gas-film controlled, while oxygen in water is liquid-film controlled. Explain using the resistance ratio.
quiz.a: Ammonia is very soluble, so m is small and m/k<sub>x</sub> is small; the gas resistance 1/k<sub>y</sub> dominates. Oxygen is sparingly soluble, so m is large and m/k<sub>x</sub> dominates; the liquid film controls.

quiz.q: For k<sub>y</sub> = 0.05, k<sub>x</sub> = 0.08 and m = 2, find K<sub>y</sub> and the gas-film share of the total resistance.
What happens to the interface composition if the gas-film coefficient becomes very large?
quiz.a: Gas-film resistance becomes negligible, so y<sub>i</sub> approaches y. The interface liquid composition then approaches x<sub>i</sub> = y/m.

quiz.q: If m increases while k<sub>y</sub> and k<sub>x</sub> stay fixed, which film becomes more controlling, and why?
quiz.a: The liquid resistance term m/k<sub>x</sub> grows with m, so the liquid film becomes more controlling. A larger m means lower solubility and a steeper equilibrium line.

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant design, the two-resistance picture is extended to non-ideal multicomponent mixtures, reactive solvents and interfacial turbulence. Modern rate-based simulators solve the same two film equations at every tray or packed segment, with mass and heat transfer coupled. Search for rate-based distillation, Maxwell-Stefan mass transfer, and enhancement factor.
